**🎯 Today's Goal:**
Your child can independently place the chess board between two players so that it is facing the correct direction.

**✅ Lesson Success Criteria:**
- Child checks the bottom-right corner before placing pieces.
- Child can verbally repeat the rule "Light on Right."
- Child correctly identifies if a board is set up wrong.

*(Purpose: "Can I teach this today?" Yes. This is a foundational 5-minute lesson.)*

---

parent_reference.heading: 2. Definition
parent_reference.content:
Board orientation refers to the correct physical placement of the chess board between two players. A board is correctly oriented when the square in each player's bottom-right corner is a light-colored square. 

---

parent_reference.heading: 3. Why It Matters
parent_reference.content:
Playing with the board turned the wrong way changes the colors of the squares where the King and Queen start. If the board is sideways, "Queen on her own color" places the pieces on the wrong files, which breaks the rules of opening theory and notation. Every chess rule assumes the board is oriented correctly first.

---

parent_reference.heading: 4. Before You Teach (Graph)
parent_reference.content:
**Prerequisites:**
- ✓ Chess Board (TOP-001)

**What this unlocks:**
- ✓ Initial Position (TOP-015)

---

parent_reference.heading: 5. Parent Understands
parent_reference.content:
*This section is for YOUR understanding. Read it, absorb it.*

A chess board is perfectly symmetrical — an 8x8 grid of alternating squares. Because of this, it is very easy to place it sideways. If you rotate an empty board 90 degrees, it looks exactly the same... except the corner colors flip.

When you sit at the board, look at the corner square closest to your right hand. **That square must be light-colored.** If it is dark-colored, the board is sideways. Since the board is symmetrical, if the square on your right is light, the square on your opponent's right will also be light. 

---

parent_reference.heading: 6. How to Teach It
parent_reference.content:
*Now that you understand the concept, here is exactly how to explain it to your child.*

### Step 1 — The Empty Board (1 min)
Place the empty board between you and your child, intentionally placing it sideways so a dark square is on the right.
> *"Look at this board. It looks ready, right? But it's actually hiding a secret mistake!"*

### Step 2 — Teach the Rule (2 mins)
Hold up your right hand. Ask your child to hold up their right hand.
> *"In chess, your right hand is very important. Look down at the corner square closest to your right hand. Tap it. What color is it?"*
*(They will say dark).*
> *"Ah! The golden rule of chess is **'Light on Right.'** We have to turn the board so that a light square is under our right hand."*

### Step 3 — The Spin (1 min)
Rotate the board 90 degrees.
> *"Tap your right corner again. What color is it now? Light! Now the board is ready for the armies."*

---

parent_reference.heading: 7. Teaching Story / Analogy / Memory Hint
parent_reference.content:
> **☀️ The Sunrise Rule**
> 
> Imagine the chess board is a kingdom that wakes up when the sun rises. The sun always rises on the **right side** of the kingdom, making that corner **bright and light**. If the right corner is dark, it means the sun hasn't come up yet and the armies are still asleep! We always need the light on the right to start the game.
>
> **Memory Trick:**
> **"Light on Right"** (Rhyming makes it stick instantly).

---

parent_reference.heading: 8. Did You Know? 🎓
parent_reference.content:
In official chess tournaments, if a game starts with the board turned sideways, the rules say the game must be stopped, the board rotated correctly, and all the pieces transferred to the new board exactly as they were! It's such an important rule that even professional referees have to enforce it.

---

parent_reference.heading: 9. Board Diagram 1 — Basic Concept
parent_reference.content:
**Light on Right**

![DGM-001 Light On Right](../../assets/diagrams/TOP-002/DGM-001_Light_On_Right.svg)
*The highlighted squares show the bottom-right corner for both White and Black. Notice they are both light squares.*

---

parent_reference.heading: 10. How It Works
parent_reference.content:
Because the board alternates colors, a light square on White's bottom-right (h1) guarantees a light square on Black's bottom-right (a8). You only ever need to check your own corner. If your right corner is light, your opponent's right corner is also light. 

---

parent_reference.heading: 11. Board Diagram 2 — Practical Example
parent_reference.content:
**Wrong Orientation (Dark on Right)**

![DGM-002 Wrong Orientation](../../assets/diagrams/TOP-002/DGM-002_Wrong_Orientation.svg)
*If the board is placed like this, a dark square is in the bottom-right corner. The board must be rotated 90 degrees before setting up the pieces.*

---

parent_reference.heading: 12. Real Game Example
parent_reference.content:
If you watch any chess stream or video, notice how the players often tap or adjust the corners of the board before a match begins. They are subconsciously checking the orientation. Grandmasters do this entirely by habit — they feel uncomfortable if the board is sideways because the entire "map" of the game feels wrong in their heads.

---

parent_reference.heading: 13. Common Mistakes
parent_reference.content:
### Chess Mistakes
- ❌ **Setting up pieces first** — Putting all the pieces on the board before checking the corners. If the board is wrong, you have to take all 32 pieces off to rotate it!

### Teaching Mistakes
- ❌ **Using letters/numbers to teach orientation** — Saying "The a1 square must be black" is technically true, but too complicated for a child. Stick to "Light on Right."

> **🧑‍🏫 Coach Tip:**
> If you have a roll-up vinyl board, the coordinates (a-h, 1-8) are printed on the edges. The letters (a,b,c...) should always face the players, and the numbers (1,2,3...) should run up the sides. If the numbers are facing you, the board is sideways!

---

parent_reference.heading: 14. Teaching Notes
parent_reference.content:
- **Make it physical:** Have the child literally tap the square with their right hand. Physical touch builds memory faster than just looking.
- **Signs they understand:** They sit down at a sideways board and immediately rotate it before opening the piece box.
- **Signs of confusion:** They confuse their left and right hands. If this happens, put a sticker or a bracelet on their right hand.

> **🧑‍🏫 Coach Tip:**
> Never fix the board for them before they sit down. Deliberately set it up wrong sometimes just to see if they catch it. It builds confidence when they can correct the adult!

---

parent_reference.heading: 15. Parent FAQ
parent_reference.content:
**Q: My board has no coordinates printed on it. How do I know which way is up?**
A: That's exactly why we use "Light on Right"! As long as the bottom-right corner is a light square, the board is perfectly oriented. You don't need printed coordinates to play chess.

**Q: My child keeps confusing left and right. What should I do?**
A: Put a small piece of tape or a washable marker dot on their right hand. Say, "The hand with the dot goes to the light square."

**Q: We set up all the pieces and then realized the board was sideways. Can we just play anyway?**
A: It is highly recommended to fix it. Playing on a sideways board ruins the "Queen on her color" rule and makes learning chess notation impossible later.

---

parent_reference.heading: 16. Practice Together
parent_reference.content:
### 🔄 The Spin Game
Take an empty board. Have your child close their eyes. You spin the board (either 90 degrees, 180 degrees, or not at all). Tell them to open their eyes and shout "Ready!" if it's correct, or "Spin!" if it's wrong. Let them spin it to fix it.

### 🪞 Opposite Sides
![DGM-003 Opposite Sides](../../assets/diagrams/TOP-002/DGM-003_Opposite_Sides.svg)
Sit across from each other. Ask your child to point to their right-hand corner. Then ask them to point to YOUR right-hand corner. Show them that both corners are the same color.

---

parent_reference.heading: 17. Coach Challenge ⭐
parent_reference.content:
### 🏆 The Detective Check
**Challenge your child:**
> "I am going to try to trick you. I'm going to set up the board before you get to the table. Your job is to be the Chess Detective. If I set it up wrong, you get a point. If you don't catch me, I get a point!"

For the next 5 times you play chess, intentionally place the board sideways 3 of those times. When they sit down, wait to see if they check the corner. When they catch you, act exaggeratedly disappointed that your trick didn't work.

---

parent_reference.heading: 18. Try It Yourself
parent_reference.content:
### 🟢 Recognition (Easy)
Look at the empty board below. Is this board ready for a game of chess?

![DGM-004 Puzzle](../../assets/diagrams/TOP-002/DGM-004_Puzzle.svg)
*Answer: No! The highlighted corner on the right is dark. The board needs to be rotated.*

### 🟡 Application (Medium)
You sit down at a board. The square on your bottom-LEFT is a dark square. Is the board facing the right way?
*Answer: Yes. If the bottom-left is dark, the bottom-right must be light! "Light on Right" is fulfilled.*

### 🔴 Challenge (Hard)
![DGM-005 Puzzle Solution](../../assets/diagrams/TOP-002/DGM-005_Puzzle_Solution.svg)
If you turn a correctly oriented board completely upside down (180 degrees), is it still correctly oriented?
*Answer: Yes! Because of the checkerboard pattern, spinning the board twice (180 degrees) keeps a light square in the bottom right corner.*

---

parent_reference.content:

parent_reference.heading: 21. Parent Confidence Check ✅
parent_reference.content:
- [ ] Do I understand the "Light on Right" rule?
- [ ] Can I instantly spot if a board is sideways?
- [ ] Did my child physically touch the right-hand corner during the lesson?
- [ ] Can my child identify a sideways board?
- [ ] Does my child know that both players have a light square on their right?

**✅ If most answers are "Yes":** Congratulations — move on to **Files (TOP-003)** or **Ranks (TOP-004)**.
**🔄 If several answers are "No":** Play the "Spin Game" in Section 16 a few more times.

Take an empty board. Have your child close their eyes. You spin the board (either 90 degrees, 180 degrees, or not at all). Tell them to open their eyes and shout "Ready!" if it's correct, or "Spin!" if it's wrong. Let them spin it to fix it.

### 🪞 Opposite Sides

Sit across from each other. Ask your child to point to their right-hand corner. Then ask them to point to YOUR right-hand corner. Show them that both corners are the same color.

guide_sections.title: Coach Challenge ⭐
guide_sections.text:
### 🏆 The Detective Check
**Challenge your child:**
> "I am going to try to trick you. I'm going to set up the board before you get to the table. Your job is to be the Chess Detective. If I set it up wrong, you get a point. If you don't catch me, I get a point!"

For the next 5 times you play chess, intentionally place the board sideways 3 of those times. When they sit down, wait to see if they check the corner. When they catch you, act exaggeratedly disappointed that your trick didn't work.

guide_sections.title: Try It Yourself
guide_sections.text:
### 🟢 Recognition (Easy)
Look at the empty board below. Is this board ready for a game of chess?

*Answer: No! The highlighted corner on the right is dark. The board needs to be rotated.*

### 🟡 Application (Medium)
You sit down at a board. The square on your bottom-LEFT is a dark square. Is the board facing the right way?
*Answer: Yes. If the bottom-left is dark, the bottom-right must be light! "Light on Right" is fulfilled.*

### 🔴 Challenge (Hard)

If you turn a correctly oriented board completely upside down (180 degrees), is it still correctly oriented?
*Answer: Yes! Because of the checkerboard pattern, spinning the board twice (180 degrees) keeps a light square in the bottom right corner.*

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.text:
- **Topic**: Board Orientation
- **Difficulty**: Beginner
- **Typical age**: 6+
- **Estimated teaching time**: 5-10 min
- **Piece/concept type**: Concept
- **Prerequisites**: Chess Board (TOP-001)

**🎯 Today's Goal:**
Your child can independently place the chess board between two players so that it is facing the correct direction.

**✅ Lesson Success Criteria:**
- Child checks the bottom-right corner before placing pieces.
- Child can verbally repeat the rule "Light on Right."
- Child correctly identifies if a board is set up wrong.

*(Purpose: "Can I teach this today?" Yes. This is a foundational 5-minute lesson.)*

sections.title: Definition
sections.text: Board orientation refers to the correct physical placement of the chess board between two players. A board is correctly oriented when the square in each player's bottom-right corner is a light-colored square.

sections.title: Why It Matters
sections.text: Playing with the board turned the wrong way changes the colors of the squares where the King and Queen start. If the board is sideways, "Queen on her own color" places the pieces on the wrong files, which breaks the rules of opening theory and notation. Every chess rule assumes the board is oriented correctly first.

sections.title: Parent Understands
sections.text:
*This section is for YOUR understanding. Read it, absorb it.*

A chess board is perfectly symmetrical — an 8x8 grid of alternating squares. Because of this, it is very easy to place it sideways. If you rotate an empty board 90 degrees, it looks exactly the same... except the corner colors flip.

When you sit at the board, look at the corner square closest to your right hand. **That square must be light-colored.** If it is dark-colored, the board is sideways. Since the board is symmetrical, if the square on your right is light, the square on your opponent's right will also be light.

sections.title: How to Teach It
sections.text:
*Now that you understand the concept, here is exactly how to explain it to your child.*

### Step 1 — The Empty Board (1 min)
Place the empty board between you and your child, intentionally placing it sideways so a dark square is on the right.
> *"Look at this board. It looks ready, right? But it's actually hiding a secret mistake!"*

### Step 2 — Teach the Rule (2 mins)
Hold up your right hand. Ask your child to hold up their right hand.
> *"In chess, your right hand is very important. Look down at the corner square closest to your right hand. Tap it. What color is it?"*
*(They will say dark).*
> *"Ah! The golden rule of chess is **'Light on Right.'** We have to turn the board so that a light square is under our right hand."*

### Step 3 — The Spin (1 min)
Rotate the board 90 degrees.
> *"Tap your right corner again. What color is it now? Light! Now the board is ready for the armies."*

sections.title: Teaching Story / Analogy / Memory Hint
sections.text:
> **☀️ The Sunrise Rule**
> 
> Imagine the chess board is a kingdom that wakes up when the sun rises. The sun always rises on the **right side** of the kingdom, making that corner **bright and light**. If the right corner is dark, it means the sun hasn't come up yet and the armies are still asleep! We always need the light on the right to start the game.
>
> **Memory Trick:**
> **"Light on Right"** (Rhyming makes it stick instantly).

sections.title: Did You Know? 🎓
sections.text: In official chess tournaments, if a game starts with the board turned sideways, the rules say the game must be stopped, the board rotated correctly, and all the pieces transferred to the new board exactly as they were! It's such an important rule that even professional referees have to enforce it.

**Light on Right**

*The highlighted squares show the bottom-right corner for both White and Black. Notice they are both light squares.*

sections.title: How It Works
sections.text: Because the board alternates colors, a light square on White's bottom-right (h1) guarantees a light square on Black's bottom-right (a8). You only ever need to check your own corner. If your right corner is light, your opponent's right corner is also light.

sections.text:
**Wrong Orientation (Dark on Right)**

*If the board is placed like this, a dark square is in the bottom-right corner. The board must be rotated 90 degrees before setting up the pieces.*

sections.title: Real Game Example
sections.text: If you watch any chess stream or video, notice how the players often tap or adjust the corners of the board before a match begins. They are subconsciously checking the orientation. Grandmasters do this entirely by habit — they feel uncomfortable if the board is sideways because the entire "map" of the game feels wrong in their heads.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.text:
### Chess Mistakes
- ❌ **Setting up pieces first** — Putting all the pieces on the board before checking the corners. If the board is wrong, you have to take all 32 pieces off to rotate it!

### Teaching Mistakes
- ❌ **Using letters/numbers to teach orientation** — Saying "The a1 square must be black" is technically true, but too complicated for a child. Stick to "Light on Right."

> **🧑‍🏫 Coach Tip:**
> If you have a roll-up vinyl board, the coordinates (a-h, 1-8) are printed on the edges. The letters (a,b,c...) should always face the players, and the numbers (1,2,3...) should run up the sides. If the numbers are facing you, the board is sideways!

sections.title: Teaching Notes
sections.text:
- **Make it physical:** Have the child literally tap the square with their right hand. Physical touch builds memory faster than just looking.
- **Signs they understand:** They sit down at a sideways board and immediately rotate it before opening the piece box.
- **Signs of confusion:** They confuse their left and right hands. If this happens, put a sticker or a bracelet on their right hand.

> **🧑‍🏫 Coach Tip:**
> Never fix the board for them before they sit down. Deliberately set it up wrong sometimes just to see if they catch it. It builds confidence when they can correct the adult!

sections.title: Parent FAQ
sections.text:
**Q: My board has no coordinates printed on it. How do I know which way is up?**
A: That's exactly why we use "Light on Right"! As long as the bottom-right corner is a light square, the board is perfectly oriented. You don't need printed coordinates to play chess.

**Q: My child keeps confusing left and right. What should I do?**
A: Put a small piece of tape or a washable marker dot on their right hand. Say, "The hand with the dot goes to the light square."

**Q: We set up all the pieces and then realized the board was sideways. Can we just play anyway?**
A: It is highly recommended to fix it. Playing on a sideways board ruins the "Queen on her color" rule and makes learning chess notation impossible later.
